summary: The article covers a scandal in which AOG Aerospace, a UK parts distributor founded by Venezuelan Jose Zamora in 2015, is accused of falsifying records to pass off old or unapproved jet engine parts as genuine. CFM, a GE and Safran joint venture, is suing AOG in Britain's High Court. Experts note that post-COVID parts shortages created ideal conditions for unscrupulous sellers, and that distributors remain lightly regulated despite past fatal incidents involving counterfeit parts.
one_line: CFM is suing UK distributor AOG in the High Court over alleged falsified paperwork on jet engine parts, raising concerns about weak distributor regulation.
key_facts: CFM, a joint venture between GE and Safran that manufactures engines, is pursuing a legal case against AOG in Britain's High Court; the case began on September 21 and is ongoing.
Zamora, who is Venezuelan, started in aviation in 2010 as an account manager at AJW, an engine maintenance business, and founded AOG in 2015 from a rented terraced house in Hove.
AOG's registered address moved between four homes in three years, shifting from Hove to London in 2017, and later to serviced offices in central London.
AOG's net assets were £22,000 ($42,000) in 2019 but it was worth £2.2 million by early 2020.
In 2020 AOG won a deal with logistics firm B&H Worldwide to distribute parts from its hub in Frankfurt.

AOG is understood to have sold mainly smaller parts such as bolts, nuts, washers, dampers and seals, which carry no serial number and are harder to trace; some turbine blades have also been flagged by CFM as suspect.
CFM is understood to believe AOG passed off old parts as new.
CFM has had to audit more than 500 suppliers to find which items could be caught up in the crisis.
The parts identified so far are not thought to include life-limited parts, which operate under the most stress in a jet engine.
Partnair Flight 394 crashed off Denmark in September 1989, killing all 55 aboard, after three of four bolts holding its tail fin were counterfeit.

Mary Schiavo, US Department of Transportation inspector general in the early 1990s, helped secure more than a hundred criminal convictions over unapproved parts; unapproved parts were found in Air Force One's fire control system in 1995.
Schiavo warns that distributors are not heavily regulated, unlike manufacturers, pilots and aviation companies, and says her 1990s push for tighter rules was ignored.
The UK Civil Aviation Authority is supporting the US FAA and European Aviation Safety Agency in investigating the matter.
